The present work is the artist's proof cast prior to the casting of the edition of 12 by the Tallix Foundry in Beacon, New York.

Another example of Icarus in patinated plaster with metallic patination from the 1945 casting can be found in the collection of the Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C. (object no. 1989.29).

Donald De Lue was awarded a medal of honor at the Allied Artists of America's Thirty-Third Annual Exhibition in 1946 for Icarus.

The story of Icarus is a cautionary legend in Greek mythology. Icarus's father, Daedalus, was an inventor who was the mastermind behind King Minos's labyrinth in Crete. According to some accounts, once Theseus escaped successfully from Daedalus's concoction, King Minos ordered the creator and his son to be thrown into prison. Determined to escape, Daedalus forged two sets of wings out of feathers and beeswax. He urged his son to not fly too close to the sun as the heat would destroy the wings. Icarus ignored his father, soared up to the sun's rays and the wings fell apart. He plummeted into the sea where he tragically drowned.

Icarus is often regarded as Donald De Lue's best work. It is difficult to pinpoint exactly when the sculptor began and ultimately finalized the model. De Lue personally believed he began to conceive of the work in 1934, after his marriage to Martha Naomi Cross (1906-1982), and may have continued reworking the piece until the mid-1940s.

Icarus masterfully captures its namesake's sheer terror of plunging down as his makeshift wings come undone. The figure's compressed raised hands and feet enhance the drama and a cloud at the base further emphasizes this dramatic descent. Icarus boasts De Lue's distinctive musculature style as well as his trademark figuration on the face.

PROPERTY FROM THE COLLECTION OF MILTON AND JACQUELINE ESTEROW, NEW YORKCHARLES EPHRAIM BURCHFIELD (1893-1967)
Dusk 
bears C.E. Burchfield Foundation stamp (lower right)
watercolor and graphite on paper
17 1/2 x 30 in. (44.4 x 76.2 cm.)
Executed circa 1926.

Provenance
Estate of the artist.
Kennedy Galleries, New York.
Acquired by the late owners from the above, August 19, 1982.

Exhibited
New York, DC Moore Gallery, Charles Burchfield: Fifty Years as a Painter, June 10–September 25, 2010, pp. 70, 116, no. 28, illustrated.

This lot is accompanied by a research report completed by Nancy Weekly, Burchfield Scholar, Head of Collections & Charles Cary Rumsey Curator of the Burchfield Penney Art Center, Buffalo, New York. We wish to thank her for her kind assistance cataloging this lot.

Charles Burchfield's artistic career can be divided into three major periods: his early works, executed until about 1918, which focused on childhood memory and fantasy; works produced between 1918 and 1943 that explored themes of Social Realism; and, after 1943, a return to his early subject matter, reimagined and infused "with a kind of ecstatic poetry." (M. Baigell, Charles Burchfield, New York, 1976, p. 54) The present work, executed around 1926, originates from Burchfield's second period. In Dusk, Burchfield turns his attention to the transitional moment between day and night, capturing the sun as it hovers just above the horizon. The landscape is distilled into a dramatic arrangement of dark, silhouetted trees set against successive bands of purple, red, orange, and blue that suffuse the sky. This reductive approach to form, coupled with an evocative atmospheric palette, is characteristic of a number of works from this period in Burchfield's oeuvre, including Village in the Swamps (1930, Munson Museum of Art, Utica, New York, 57.108) and The Evening Star (1923-26, Burchfield Penney Art Center, Buffalo, New York).

Untitled 
signed 'AUGUSTUS VINCENT TACK' (lower left)
oil on canvas laid down on board
14 x 40 in. (35.6 x 101.6 cm.)
Painted circa 1930s.

Provenance
Duncan Phillips (1886-1966), Washington, D.C.
Minnie Hudson Byers (1890-1965), Washington, D.C., gift from the above. 
By descent to the late owners within the family of the above.

Augustus Vincent Tack's abstractions of the late 1920s and 1930s represent a distinct unification of landscape, symbolism, and spiritual expression within the development of American modernism. Tack's approach was deeply personal and remained somewhat apart from the prevailing principles of American modernism, drawing upon his encounters with the American West, particularly the Rocky Mountains, whose monumental scale and dramatic atmospheric effects provided an important impetus for his approach to the abstract. In the present work, the suggestion of a mountainous landscape remains discernible in the serrated peaks and receding planes that dominate the composition, yet the subject has been radically transformed through flattened areas of blue, violet, rose, and ochre. Delineated by sinuous, calligraphic contours, these forms appear to shift between solid land, atmospheric phenomena, and pure color, while luminous passages of gold permeating the upper portion further dissolve the boundary between landscape and abstraction and lend the work a sublime quality. 

Central to Tack's artistic development was his relationship with Duncan Phillips (1886–1966), whom he first met in 1914 and with whom he formed a lifelong friendship. Phillips became Tack's earliest and most important patron, advocating for an artist whose abstractions did not readily conform to prevailing expectations of modern painting. In 1928, Phillips commissioned Tack to create a series of monumental abstractions for a large gallery at his museum, now known as the Music Room, a project that occupied Tack until 1931. (L. Furth, Augustus Vincent Tack: Landscape of the Spirit, exhibition catalogue, Washington, D.C., 1993, p. 84.) The resulting works, which Tack revered as the crowning achievement of his career, embodied Phillips's conception of art as a vehicle for spiritual and emotional experience through their fragmented forms, luminous color, and dynamic rhythms. The present work belongs to this important period, when Tack was refining a visual language in which recognizable landscape motifs were progressively subordinated to the expressive relationships of color, contour, light, and space.

The present work was presented as a gift by Phillips to Minnie Hudson Byers (1890–1965), a longtime member of Phillips' circle who played an important role in the development and administration of The Phillips Collection. Byers began working for the Phillips family in 1918, initially providing financial advice to Duncan Phillips' mother, and later served as treasurer of the museum. As such, the passage of the present work directly from Phillips to Byers is particularly evocative, as it places the painting within the intimate personal and institutional network that supported Tack's unconventional vision of American abstraction during the 1930s. The present work is not only tied to one of Tack's most important advocates but also to a woman whose contributions were integral to the early history of The Phillips Collection.

Beginning in the 1910s, John Marin turned to coastal Maine as a retreat from the energy and congestion of New York, and by the 1920s, the region's houses, islands, waterways, boats, and villages—particularly Stonington—had become vehicles for his increasingly experimental explorations of space, line, and color. In his watercolors depicting Maine during this period, Marin frequently employed an elevated viewpoint, compressing foreground, middle ground, and distance into a shallow, interconnected plane. Charcoal lines vigorously define the elements of the landscape, while watercolor washes alternately reinforce and dissolve those contours. This interplay between drawing and watercolor allowed Marin to retain the recognizable features of a particular landscape while conveying its changing rhythms and sensations.

Village, Maine, executed in 1923, is a particularly accomplished example of this approach. Likely depicting Stonington, Maine, an important subject for Marin throughout his artistic career and where he spent the summer of 1923, the composition is constructed from an elevated perspective, allowing the village to coalesce into a vibrant arrangement of intersecting roads, architectural forms, trees, and hills. The church and its steeple provide a visual anchor, while the roadway and irregular bands of land lead the eye diagonally through the scene. Throughout the foreground, broad passages of blue, green, brown, and gray are punctuated by vigorous charcoal contours, abbreviated forms, and flashes of more intense color. Equally integral to the composition is the exposed paper, interrupting the washes and contributing to the watercolor's sense of spontaneity and movement. Marin's forms appear to oscillate between definition and dissolution, as Sheldon Reich notes of his depictions of Stonington, "Marin's stylistic treatment of the village varies and ranges from the abstract to a fairly straightforward visual rendition." (S. Reich, John Marin : A Stylistic Analysis and Catalogue Raisonné, Tucson, Arizona, vol. I, p. 140)

In Village, Maine, Marin also employs his "frame within a frame" or internal framing technique derived from Cubist principles. The strong, angular charcoal lines that define the edges of the composition impose structure against the abstracted forms, emphasizing Marin's approach to space as both illusionistic and flat. Marin takes this framing technique a degree further by physically anchoring the sheet onto a much larger sheet that acts as a border and that extends his framing designs in both charcoal and watercolor. The layering of the sheets creates spatial depth while underscoring the work's fundamentally two-dimensional character. Reich observes that, "The frame within a frame forms a strong, flat plane through which we drop back into the illusionist space of the view beyond. On the other hand...the vigorous abstract shape of the frame itself adds an independent interest to the picture." (S. Reich, John Marin : A Stylistic Analysis and Catalogue Raisonné, pp. 147-48) Furthermore, Marin's framing technique dismantles both the conventional rectangular frame format and the physical boundaries of the sheet, allowing his washes and designs to spill beyond their prescribed limits.

Village, Maine exemplifies the artistic innovations Marin developed during the 1920s, a decade in which his depictions of coastal Maine became increasingly experimental in their treatment of space, form, and color. Rooted in the recognizable landscape of Stonington yet moving beyond conventional modes of representation, the present work brings together the interrelated concerns that defined Marin's work of this period: observation and abstraction, spatial depth and planar structure, and delineation and dissolution. In fusing a specific sense of place with formal experimentation, Village, Maine demonstrates Marin's distinctive approach to rhythm, color, and form and the central role that Maine played in its evolution.

Gaston Lachaise's Standing Woman (Standing Woman with Knee on Pedestal) [LF 177], was first documented in March 1927, when the initial, highly-polished bronze cast was exhibited in his show at Alfred Stieglitz's The Intimate Gallery, New York. It was bought by a private collector very soon after the exhibition closed in early April, and Lachaise obtained a copyright for the work on April 30. The support for the woman's raised leg in the statuette has been described as a pedestal, but the copyright registration calls it a stool, and the drapery, a scarf, suggesting everyday accessories. The woman's powerful, voluptuous body and her confident bearing closely compare, for example, to those of the partly draped female in his sculpture known as Biggest Woman in the World [LF 127], which was modeled in about 1917 and first cast by 1931 (Norton Museum of Art, West Palm Beach, Florida). Potent figures such as these symbolize Lachaise's personal vision of America's extraordinary vitality and potential.

The initial cast, last documented in 1969, is said to be inscribed with Lachaise's signature and a copyright date of 1924. Although Lachaise dated the cast 1927 in his list of sculptures for his 1935 retrospective exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, where it appeared, it is instead dated 1924 in the show's catalogue, and that year has commonly been assigned to the work since then. Four or perhaps five other casts have been made. An unsigned, undated bronze authorized by Lachaise's widow in 1955, produced by the Modern Art Foundry, and exhibited from 1962 to 1963 in a traveling exhibition organized by the Museum of Modern Art, New York, is in a private collection. Two more casts were made in about 1961. These are evidently the unsigned, undated Roman Bronze Works Inc. cast owned by the Kitchener-Waterloo Art Gallery, Kitchener, Ontario; and the cast inscribed with Lachaise's signature and a copyright date of 1934 (reworked from 1927 during the casting process) that is on loan to the Yale University Art Gallery. Another cast, referenced in 1969, is said to be inscribed with the signature and a copyright date of 1924. The Lachaise Foundation, which was established in 1963 and authorized an edition of 10 numbered Estate casts of the work, produced only the present example thus far. A plaster model, which lacks any inscription, is owned by the Lachaise Foundation.

Joseph Stella's journey to Barbados in 1937 proved transformative, reinvigorating his engagement with the natural world and providing a source of inspiration that would occupy him for the remainder of his career. Drawn to the island's intense sunlight, luxuriant vegetation, and vivid colors, Stella translated his experience of Barbados into a distinctive style in which observation and fantasy converge. His landscapes and floral compositions from this period are characterized by saturated hues, boldly simplified forms, and an almost dreamlike sense of space, reflecting what he regarded as the island's capacity to restore the spirit. The experience also prompted a renewed interest in the human figure, often placing solitary or monumental figures within richly colored tropical settings. In Tropicalia, painted in 1940, a seated woman viewed from behind occupies the foreground, her monumental form set against a rhythmic arrangement of exotic foliage, bands of sea and sky, and brilliantly colored vegetation. The contrast between the figure's dark, earthy presence and the luminous landscape surrounding her heightens the painting's sensuality while demonstrating Stella's characteristic ability to transform the observed world into a highly personal vision. Though Stella remained in Barbados for only five months, he absorbed motifs that would inspire his art for the next three years, producing paintings that radiated with the innocent sensuality that Stella associated with the "ardor of youth." (B. Haskell, Joseph Stella, exhibition catalogue, New York, 1994, p. 175) The Barbados works ultimately represent one of the most exuberant and imaginative chapters of Stella's career, and Tropicalia exemplifies the fusion of nature, color, and fantasy that defined this late period.

After studying at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia, William Hunt Diederich and fellow student and sculptor, Paul Manship (1885-1966), "Took off for Spain in 1908. Trekking through Andalusia that summer, they spent the month of July drawing and modeling, usually sleeping on beaches and roadsides to conserve the $40 they had for their trip." (J.C. Connor, J. Rosenkranz, Rediscoveries in American Sculpture, New York, 1989, p. 20) Diederich was greatly inspired by his travels in Spain and went on to produce several Spanish-themed sculptures during his career, including the present work and, most notably, Muletier Espagnol, a bronze group that he exhibited at the 1911 Paris Salon. In 1920, Spanish Rider (El Majo) was selected for Diederich's first one-man exhibition hosted by Kingore Galleries. Represented by eighty-eight different sculptures and decorative works, the exhibition reflected Diederich's interest in animal and human forms, alone or combined.

The present work depicts "A beautiful hemlock with a growth of goldenrod and asters at its feet" in the rural, secluded landscape surrounding Zimmerman Road outside the town of Boston, New York where Charles Ephraim Burchfield famously painted numerous times throughout his artistic career. (C.E. Burchfield, Journals, September 20, 1954, vol. 55, pp. 110-14) According to Nancy Weekly, "Wind Blown Hemlock is related to two watercolor paintings with the same title, one painted in 1954 and the other, a smaller version, in 1955. Charles E. Burchfield signed and dated this drawing, thus giving it autonomy. One cannot be certain whether he produced the drawing in situ as a study before painting the 1954 watercolor or whether he reproduced the basic structure of the composition afterwards; yet one is inclined to believe the latter." This lot is accompanied by a letter dated September 6, 2026, from Marie Louise Kane, scholar on the work of Richard Edward Miller and author of the monograph, A Bright Oasis: The Paintings of Richard E. Miller. We wish to thank Marie Louise Kane for providing the following essay.

Woman Sewing, circa 1927, was painted by Richard E. Miller in Provincetown, Massachusetts. It belongs to a genre–comely women in a private interior corner, contemplatively engaged in a simple task–that is classic Miller, one he developed with great success in France in the 1910s before the outbreak of World War I. When the war broke out, Miller, like thousands of foreign artists, returned to his own country, intending to return when hostilities had ended. With his wife and small daughter he first went back to his hometown, St. Louis, Missouri, where portrait orders poured in. In the spring of 1916 he was, in his words, "still grinding them out," but had his eye on the West Coast. September found him warmly heralded in California, giving painting instruction at the newly founded (1914) Stickney Memorial School of Fine Arts in Pasadena. Despite success there, Miller didn't take to California and by August 1917, he joined several of his former colleagues in Provincetown, Massachusetts, a growing art colony started by his friend Charles Webster Hawthorne (1872-1930), whose outdoor painting classes began there in 1899. American Art News (Aug. 18, 1917, p. 3) took note: "Richard Miller has just joined the colony for the reason that it brings him a little nearer to France." Although Miller returned briefly to his old studio in Brittany in 1922, he settled in Provincetown for the rest of his life, continuing his successful career. Upon his death Art Digest (Vol. 17, Feb. 1, 1943, p. 14) stated that he was, "best known for his beautifully finished figure painting in the conservative tradition."

Woman Sewing was painted during a period of artistic fomentation in Provincetown. Miller was an outspoken critic of the modern tendencies (abstraction) that began splitting the art colony into two camps. By 1927 the Provincetown Art Association was compelled by pressure from its younger members, who felt excluded from the association's annual exhibitions, to hold two annual exhibitions–one for each camp, "modern" and "regular." Miller was very much at the center of this split and may have felt he had the last laugh when a "hoax" he painted and signed with a fake name was hung in the modern section of the 1926 annual. Miller continued as a successful painter for another fifteen years, holding to his belief that, "Art's mission is not literary, the telling of a story, but decorative, the conveying of a pleasant optical sensation."

Two features of Woman Sewing indicate that it was painted in Provincetown: the bow-back Windsor chair and the blue painted French windows. The tall, double-casement windows were part of Miller's Provincetown studio, as well as the chair, as seen in period photos of it. The white, tiered skirt and the floral drape are props familiar from earlier Miller paintings–the white skirt appearing in his French paintings, and the floral drape first appearing in a California painting. A study of Miller's oeuvre reveals a penchant for incorporating certain objects repeatedly, with variation, in his work. What mattered to him was composition, color, and texture and the way light affected objects–offering infinitely variable aesthetic possibilities. The houses seen in the background are Provincetown houses. Miller took liberties with their colors (as did the Provincetown Printmakers of the period) to suit his aesthetic purpose. The pale pink, yellow, and gray tones harmonize with his interior elements. These pastel hues were no doubt sparked by Miller's time in the West Indies, where he had given painting instruction earlier in the year.

Literature

M.A. Burke, Elizabeth Nourse, 1859-1938: A Salon Career, Washington, D.C., 1983, pp. 58-59, 84.

Mary Cassatt repeatedly explored the motif of mother and child throughout her oeuvre. Although she never married or had children, her intimate depictions of motherhood became her most widely recognized subject. Cassatt often depicted women in public and private settings and frequently captured familiar interactions between mothers and young children. By the turn of the twentieth century, Cassatt devoted particular attention to scenes of domesticity, a focus to which Baby Charles: Head and Arms speaks.

Cassatt was born in Allegheny, Pennsylvania, in 1844. As a teenager, she began taking classes at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts before moving to Europe to further her artistic training. She became the only American artist to join the Impressionist group in Paris, where she would work and exhibit alongside the likes of Edgar Degas (1834-1917) and Camille Pissarro (1830-1903), among others. It was in Paris in the late 1870s that Cassatt's mastery of pastel began to develop.

Cassatt wrote that pastel was, "the most satisfactory medium for [portraying] children." Harriet K. Stratis observes, "It may have been the velvety and tactile qualities of the medium that led her to associate its use with the depiction of youth. The spontaneity that pastel allowed was surely an advantage when drawing children who could or would not sit still for long periods of time." (H.K. Stratis, "Innovation and Tradition in Mary Cassatt's Pastels: A Study of Her Methods and Materials," Mary Cassatt Modern Woman, exhibition catalogue, New York, p. 221) The four pastels Cassatt executed of Baby Charles offer a particularly compelling example of this spontaneity. Baby Charles (1900, Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Washington, D.C., accession no. 66.846), Baby Charles Looking Over His Mother's Shoulder (No. 1), Baby Charles Looking Over His Mother's Shoulder (No. 2) (circa 1900, Private collection, Paris, France) and the present work record subtle variations in the child's expression and, most notably, the placement of his hands. In the present work, the child is placed caringly over his mother's right shoulder, with his arms dangling freely as Cassatt experiments with their position. In the oil Baby Charles Looking Over His Mother's Shoulder (No. 3) (Thomas H. and Diane DeMell Jacobsen Ph.D. Foundation), she ultimately settles on the child's two hands touching atop his mother's shoulder. 

Cassatt's mother and child scenes date as far back as the late 1880s, but from 1900 onward, the subject assumed an increasingly central place in her work. The present work, executed in 1900, reflects Cassatt's sustained interest in the intimate relationship between mothers and children and showcases her exemplary skills as a portraitist. The present work exemplifies Cassatt's sustained interest in capturing mothers and children and showcases her exemplary skills in portraiture and as a colorist.

Baby Charles: Head and Arms was once in the collection of Elizabeth Nourse (1859-1938), another prominent female artist working at the turn of the twentieth century. Scholars believe that Cassatt may have given this pastel to Nourse in recognition of her service to the American Woman's Art Association, of which Cassatt was a member. Cassatt served as President in 1898, while Nourse served as President from 1899-1900. Their successive leadership of the Association underscores the connection between the two artists and lends particular significance to their shared artistic and professional circles.

According to Susan Hobbs, Thomas Wilmer Dewing "Modeled The Waiting Athlete after the dictum he had learned at the Académie Julian, that shadows must be massed along the outlines of limbs and torso, an effect that he emphasized with a strong side lighting. Dewing, however, gave his athlete an elegant, slender quality. His positioning of the outstretched limb and his careful articulation of the right foot would become a frequent feature of his female nudes. Likewise, the freely brushed turquoise sky that sets off the tightly painted, bronze flesh tones of the sitter foreshadows the artist's later concern for textural contrast." (S. Hobbs, Thomas Wilmer Dewing: Beauty into Art, A Catalogue Raisonné, New Haven, Connecticut, 2018, vol. I, p. 86.) Furthermore, Hobbs notes that the architectural setting of the present work "Seems stage-like and contrived, with its inclusion of a column in the middle ground next to which stands a figure in classical dress. It may, however, have been an actual place within the Académie Julian itself. The skin-covered stool, hanging wire, distant vent, and other elements suggest that the site may be a corner of a stage for models. Dewing most likely completed the panel in Boston, however, since he was in Boston in 1878, the date he gave the picture in roman numerals." (S. Hobbs, Thomas Wilmer Dewing: Beauty into Art, A Catalogue Raisonné, p. 86.)

Francis Augustus Silva remains one of the most revered American landscape painters associated with the second generation of the Hudson River School. Born in New York City in 1835, Silva began his career as a sign-painter's apprentice after several occupations and by the late 1860s, turned to a career as an artist. His first paintings were exhibited in 1868 at the National Academy of Design where his interest in marine subjects was revealed. Despite his unconventional training, Silva developed a highly refined approach to landscape painting and quickly became celebrated for his coastal and riverine views, often depicting tranquil waters, dramatic skies, and distant mountains rendered with careful attention to atmospheric effects. Silva's oeuvre belongs to the later work of the Hudson River School, when artists increasingly sought to emphasize subtle tonal harmonies and intimate observations of nature rather than producing monumental depictions of the wilderness favored by earlier proponents of the Hudson River School, such as Thomas Cole (1801-1848) and Frederic Edwin Church (1826-1900).

Focusing on quiet stretches of water and expansive skies, Silva employed a compositional restraint and delicate light effects that lend a contemplative mood to his landscapes. He was particularly adept at rendering reflections and subtle gradations of color across bodies of water, which became central stylistic techniques celebrated in his mature work. In contrast to the dramatic panoramas that characterized the works of the first generation of Hudson River School artists, Silva frequently adopted lower vantage points and horizontal compositions that emphasize the calm, yet ever-changing surface of oceans and rivers. His works often include small vessels, docks, or distant shorelines that situate human narrative within the broader natural environment. Through these elements, Silva conveyed a sense of harmony between nature and the presence of human commerce on America's beaches and shorelines.

A Summer Promenade Along the Beach at Coney Island exemplifies these qualities while also demonstrating Silva's interest in dramatic atmospheric effects. The composition presents a panoramic view of the beach at Coney Island, with gently rising dunes extending along the left and the expansive waters of the Atlantic stretching toward the horizon at right. Groups of fashionably dressed figures populate the beach, while sailing vessels and steamships can be seen in the distance traversing along the horizon. Above, clouds drift across an expansive sky, illuminated by subtle passages of warm pink and orange light filtering through the atmosphere that suggests the approach of evening. These delicate tonalities are reflected in the water below, while the frothy, rolling waves echo in form the clouds above. Silva's interplay between sea and sky creates a compositional harmony that reinforces the painting's serene atmosphere.

The present work also reflects broader themes associated with the later generation of the Hudson River School during the late nineteenth century. The juxtaposition of the natural landscape with modern vessels and structures along the shoreline, particularly the coastal resort buildings in the distance, suggests the increasing coexistence of nature and human development along New York's beaches. By this period, coastal destinations such as Coney Island had become important recreational spaces, offering respite from the heat, pollution, and congestion of the rapidly expanding city. Yet Silva does not allow these signs of modern life to overwhelm the landscape. His careful rendering of reflections and atmospheric light reinforces the contemplative character of the scene, while the diminutive scale of the figures, buildings, and distant vessels preserves the visual primacy of sea and sky. Rather than presenting the American landscape as untamed wilderness, A Summer Promenade Along the Beach at Coney Island depicts a lived-in environment shaped by both natural forces and human presence. In this way, the painting reflects the evolving vision of a later generation of Hudson River School artists, balancing a romantic sensitivity to nature with subtle acknowledgments of the industrial, commercial, and social transformations reshaping the American landscape.

William Trost Richards stands among the most accomplished American landscape and marine painters of the nineteenth century, celebrated for both his unwavering fidelity to nature and austere technical sensitivities in rendering light, atmosphere, and the diverse geography of America's coastline. Born in Philadelphia in 1833, Richards briefly studied drawing and painting with the German-born artist Paul Weber (1823–1916) before traveling to Europe from 1855 to 1856, where he encountered the traditions of European landscape painting. A formative moment in Richards' artistic development came in 1858, when he attended an exhibition of British art in Philadelphia and encountered the work of the English Pre-Raphaelites. Inspired by their example and the writings of the influential English critic John Ruskin (1819–1900), Richards increasingly embraced a careful and direct observation of nature. In 1863, he joined the Association for the Advancement of Truth in Art, an American group devoted to Ruskin's principles, whose members sought to represent the natural world with exacting fidelity. Richards' landscapes of the 1860s consequently reveal a remarkable attention to detail in rendering rocky promontories, tall grass, trees, bending rivers, and the unruly sea, while simultaneously demonstrating his evolving interest in the transient effects of light and atmosphere.

Richards' devotion to close observation distinguished his work from the more generalized and romanticized visions of nature associated with the earlier generations of the Hudson River School. Rather than relying principally upon sweeping panoramas or idealized conceptions of wilderness, Richards frequently focused his attention upon the specific physical characteristics of a particular place. Individual plants, rocks, and beaches are carefully articulated, reflecting the Ruskinian conviction that the truthful representation of nature could reveal both its beauty and its underlying order. During the 1860s, Richards brought this meticulous approach to a variety of landscape subjects, while increasingly exploring coastal scenery. The meeting of land and sea offered particularly fertile ground for his developing interests: the tangible specificity of grasses, dunes, rocks, and sandy beaches could be contrasted with the more elusive and constantly changing effects of water, clouds, and atmospheric light. By the end of the decade, these coastal subjects would assume an increasingly prominent place in Richards' oeuvre, anticipating the celebrated marine paintings that would occupy him throughout much of his later career.

Painted in 1866, Along the Shore, Rhode Island beautifully demonstrates this transitional moment in Richards' artistic development, combining the meticulous naturalism of his Pre-Raphaelite landscapes with an emerging fascination with the atmospheric possibilities of the coast. Richards organizes the composition around a narrow sandy path that begins near the lower center of the canvas and winds gently through tall coastal grasses toward a group of figures in the middle distance. The path provides both a strong compositional device and an invitation into the landscape, leading the viewer through the carefully observed foreground toward the distant shoreline and horizon. At left, the dark horizontal band of the Atlantic is punctuated by breaking white waves and several seabirds, while low dunes extend into the distance at right. Above this comparatively narrow expanse of land and sea rises an immense and dramatically illuminated sky. Dense gray clouds dominate the upper portion of the composition but are pierced near the center by brilliant sunlight and passages of blue. Rays of light descend through the clouds toward the landscape below, introducing a sense of grandeur and exaltedness to an otherwise intimate coastal scene. The small figures traveling along the path provide a subtle human narrative, yet their diminutive scale ensures that the overwhelming presence of the natural environment remains the principal subject.

Along the Shore, Rhode Island occupies an important position between Richards' exacting Pre-Raphaelite landscapes of the early and mid-1860s and the marine subjects that would increasingly command his attention throughout the remainder of his career. The finely articulated vegetation of the foreground retains Richards' Ruskinian commitment to the precise observation of nature, while the expansive sky, distant sea, and dramatic variation of sunlight anticipate his heightened interest in atmosphere and the sea that would characterize his mature work. In the present work, Richards does not present the Rhode Island coast as an untamed wilderness. Instead, the figures walking along the sandy path suggest a landscape experienced and inhabited by people, yet one in which humanity remains subordinate to the greater rhythms and forces of the natural world. The contrast between the intimacy of the foreground and the seemingly limitless expanse of sea and sky gives the painting much of its emotional power. In this way, Along the Shore, Rhode Island bridges two important currents within Richards' career: the Ruskinian conviction that truth could be discovered through the meticulous study of nature and a blossoming fascination with light, atmosphere, and the sea that would ultimately establish him as one of the foremost American marine painters of the nineteenth century.

Louis Rémy Mignot (1831-1870) occupies a distinctive position among the second generation of artists associated with the Hudson River School. Born in Charleston, South Carolina in 1831 to parents of French descent, Mignot left America as a young man for Europe to pursue his artistic education. By 1850, he had settled in The Hague, where he studied for several years under the Dutch landscape painter Andreas Schelfhout (1787-1870). Mignot's European training distinguished him from many of his American contemporaries and Schelfhout's instruction fostered in Mignot an enduring sensitivity to atmosphere, tonal harmony, and the changing effects of light. Mignot returned to America in the mid-1850s and quickly established himself in New York, where he became associated with the circle of landscape painters working in the artistic traditions of the Hudson River School championed by Thomas Cole (1801-1848) and Asher Brown Durand (1796-1886). Yet Mignot developed a highly individual approach to landscape painting. Rather than emphasizing the precise description and monumental grandeur favored by some of his contemporaries, his landscapes frequently depend upon subtle gradations of color, atmospheric effects, and evocative passages of light to convey the poetic character of the natural world.

A pivotal moment occurred in Mignot's career in 1857 when Frederic Edwin Church (1826-1900) requested that he accompany him on an extensive journey through Ecuador, where Mignot, much like Church, would find the tropical subject matter that would help solidify his reputation as one of the great landscape painters of the 19th century. Church traveled to South America for the first time in 1853 and wished to return to pursue once again the extraordinary tropical and mountainous scenery that had captured his imagination during his first voyage. Mignot joined Church on this second expedition, traveling from New York across the Isthmus of Panama and onward to Ecuador, where the two artists made numerous sketches and studies of the country's tropical lowlands, river valleys, and soaring Andean peaks of Chimborazo and Cotopaxi. Although the two artists traveled together, their responses to the South American landscape were notably different. Church frequently pursued the topographical and botanical specificity of individual sites, while Mignot demonstrated a particular sensitivity to broader atmospheric effects, often subordinating precise detail to the expressive possibilities of mist, distance, and changing light. The journey provided Mignot with a wealth of visual material that would inform his paintings for years afterward and introduced the mountain landscape as an important subject within his developing oeuvre. (V. Johnson, Glorious Country: How the Artist Frederic Church Brought the World to American and America to the World, New York, 2026, pp. 127-33)

Painted around the same year as his travels with Church, Mountain Sunset can be understood within the context of this transformative period in Mignot's career. The composition is dominated by a monumental mountain range rising dramatically across the distance, its rugged peaks silhouetted against the fading light of the evening sky. Mignot organizes the landscape through successive bands of foreground, middle distance, and mountain, creating a powerful sensation of depth as the terrain gradually recedes toward the horizon. Above, the setting sun illuminates the atmosphere with warm passages of gold, rose, and orange that dissolve gradually into cooler tonalities, while shadows gather across the lower slopes and foreground. Rather than describing every geological feature with equal precision, Mignot allows portions of the mountains to dissolve into atmospheric haze, emphasizing the changing effects of light across the landscape. The resulting contrast between the solidity of the mountain forms and the immaterial quality of the illuminated sky transforms the scene from a straightforward topographical record into a poetic meditation on the fleeting effects of sunset.

Mountain Sunset masterfully reflects the broader ideals of landscape painting often associated with the Hudson River School while simultaneously revealing the qualities that distinguish Mignot's work from that of his contemporaries. Like Church and other artists of his generation, Mignot recognized the mountain landscape as a vehicle through which to communicate the grandeur and sublimity of the natural world. Yet his emphasis on the interplay of atmospheric effects and tonal harmony produces a markedly contemplative image. The mountains remain monumental, but their forms are softened by distance and enveloped within the luminous atmosphere that becomes the true subject of the painting. If Mountain Sunset was conceived during or in the immediate aftermath of Mignot's 1857 South American journey, its treatment of mountainous terrain and dramatic evening light would strongly reflect the visual experiences he encountered while traveling through the Andes. More broadly, Mountain Sunset demonstrates Mignot's ability to unite his European artistic training with the expansive vision of American landscape painting. Through the visual relationship of mountain, shadow, and fading sunlight, Mignot transforms the observable landscape into an evocative expression of nature's transience and grandeur, qualities that would remain central to his highly individual contribution to nineteenth-century American landscape painting.

John Frederick Kensett's Scene Near Greeley, Colorado is a tour de force within the artist's oeuvre and a rare, monumental testament to his experience in the American West. In the present work, Kensett renders the expansive grandeur of the Rocky Mountain landscape of Colorado with his celebrated quietude, luminosity, and compositional refinement. One of the foremost members of the second generation of the Hudson River School, Kensett developed a highly personal approach to landscape painting in which he employed restraint, poetic suggestion, and atmospheric light over the sublime effects favored by an earlier generation—qualities that would later identify him as one of the principal exponents of American Luminism. In Scene Near Greeley, Colorado, Kensett applied this refined sensibility to the comparatively unfamiliar terrain of the American West. Rather than emphasizing the geological spectacle of the Rocky Mountains, he subordinated them to the larger harmony of the composition, creating a landscape in which the grandeur of the West is conveyed not through theatrical effect but through the measured orchestration of light, color, atmosphere, and space.

Born in Cheshire, Connecticut in 1816, Kensett received his earliest artistic training from his father, Thomas Kensett (1786–1829), an English-born engraver who immigrated to America. Following his father's death, Kensett continued his training as an engraver and by the late 1830s was working in New York and Albany, where the precision demanded by the medium sharpened his meticulous draftsmanship and sensitivity to tonal gradation. In 1840, Kensett embarked for Europe with fellow artists John William Casilear (1811–1893), Thomas Rossiter (1818–1871) and Asher B. Durand (1796–1886), remaining abroad for approximately seven years. (J.P. Driscoll, J.K. Howat, John Frederick Kensett: An American Master, exhibition catalogue, New York and London, p. 49) During this period, Kensett traveled through England, France, Germany, Switzerland and Italy, studying the European landscape tradition while developing his skills as a painter. His exposure to the work of the seventeenth-century masters, such as Claude Lorrain (1600–1682), as well as contemporary British landscape painting, provided him with an important foundation for developing his unique aesthetic and ultimately shaped his approach to landscape painting. Kensett returned to New York in 1847 and quickly began work to establish himself as one of the country's leading landscape painters, becoming an Associate of the National Academy of Design the following year and a full Academician in 1849. (J.P. Driscoll, J.K. Howat, John Frederick Kensett: An American Master, pp. 37-38)

Kensett's mature style developed from his close observation of the American landscape and from his belief that nature's most profound effects could be expressed through clarity and restraint. Like his contemporaries Frederic Edwin Church (1826–1900), Sanford Robinson Gifford (1823–1880), Worthington Whittredge (1820–1910), and Jasper Francis Cropsey (1823–1900), Kensett traveled extensively in search of subjects, painting throughout the Catskills and Adirondacks, around Lake George and Niagara Falls, and along the rocky coasts of Massachusetts, Maine, Rhode Island and Connecticut. Yet Kensett increasingly distinguished himself from the dramatic, narrative sublime associated with many of his Hudson River School contemporaries. By the 1850s and 1860s, he began simplifying his compositions, reducing landscape to carefully balanced arrangements of earth, water, and sky and suppressing anecdotal detail in favor of tonal unity. This evolution reached its fullest expression in the coastal paintings of his final years, in which glasslike expanses of water, spare shorelines, and luminous skies approach an almost abstract simplicity.

It was against this background that Kensett turned his attention toward the American West. In the summer of 1870, at the height of his reputation, Kensett traveled westward to Colorado, entering a landscape that had already assumed an almost mythic position in the American imagination. The development of the transcontinental railroad and related western rail networks made these previously remote territories increasingly accessible to artists and tourists, while paintings by Albert Bierstadt (1830–1902), Thomas Hill (1829–1908), and others introduced Eastern audiences to spectacular visions of the Rocky Mountains. Rather than reinventing his artistic identity in response to the West, Kensett carried with him the aesthetic principles he refined over decades of painting in the Northeast. His surviving Colorado studies reveal his fascination with the dry, crystalline atmosphere, broad plains, and successive mountain ranges of the region. In Mountains in Colorado (Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C., object no. 1967.136.6) and Snowy Range and Foothills from the Valley of Valmont, Colorado (Denver Art Museum, Colorado, accession no. 1975.66) of 1870, for example, Kensett rejected the familiar convention of presenting the Rockies as an overwhelming wall of peaks rising dramatically from the plains. Instead, Kensett depicts successive ridges receding toward the Continental Divide in muted browns, greens and grays. The result is characteristically Kensett: the sublimity of the subject remains intact, but spectacle is subordinated to atmosphere.

Kensett's Western journey occurred during the final and remarkably productive years of his career. His experiences in Colorado provided him with a new vocabulary of mountains, plains, and vast skies that could be reconciled with the increasingly distilled language of his late paintings. Unlike Bierstadt, whose monumental Western compositions frequently exaggerate topographical features through dramatic illumination and monumental scale, Kensett generally resisted transforming the Rocky Mountains into a theatrical protagonist. Instead, his Western landscapes emphasize distance and atmospheric recession. Mountain forms are often placed far from the viewer, their contours softened by intervening air, while the immediate foreground remains comparatively intimate and accessible, as seen in his Storm, Western Colorado (1870, Former Collection of the Toledo Museum of Art, Toledo, Ohio). This approach allowed Kensett to translate the enormous physical scale of the West into the language of Luminism while maintaining a contemplative quality central to his mature work. Kensett's Colorado paintings occupy a significant and compelling position within his oeuvre: they demonstrate how an artist whose reputation was established through images of Lake George and the Atlantic seaboard could confront an entirely different landscape and remain unmistakably true to his aesthetic and approach to landscape painting.

The setting of Scene Near Greeley, Colorado is significant, as Greeley was a remarkably new settlement when Kensett encountered the region. Established in 1869 as the Union Colony of Colorado under the leadership of Nathan Meeker (1817–1879), an agricultural reporter for the New York Tribune and named in honor of New York Tribune editor Horace Greeley (1811–1872), the settlement represented an ambitious experiment in organized Western colonization. Kensett was therefore not depicting an untouched landscape removed from contemporary American expansion, but a region undergoing rapid transformation through settlement, agriculture, irrigation, and the railroad. However, nearly all signs of this transformation, such as houses, roads, railroad tracks, settlers, and cultivated fields, are excluded from the present work. In this respect, Scene Near Greeley, Colorado does not provide an accurate topographical record, as Kensett instead reorganizes the landscape according to his aesthetic ideals, presenting the newly settled West as a realm of timeless natural harmony. Furthermore, the absence of overt narrative from the present work allows the viewer to contemplate the landscape itself—a landscape inevitably confronting the rapidly changing world just beyond the limits of Kensett's composition.

Within Kensett's small, yet important group of work produced during this period, Scene Near Greeley, Colorado stands apart for both its scale and its compositional ambition. In the present work, Kensett depicts a broad clearing near Greeley with the Rocky Mountains extending across the distant horizon, yet Kensett pointedly refuses to allow the mountains to dominate the composition. Instead, the viewer encounters the scene from within a shadowed foreground of earth, vegetation, pools of water and trees. A monumental tree rises slightly left of center, its branching trunk and spreading canopy establishing the principal vertical axis of the composition. The tree simultaneously anchors and divides the landscape: to the left, densely massed woodland closes the view, while to the right the terrain opens dramatically toward the plains and distant mountains. This juxtaposition between enclosure and openness creates the painting's underlying spatial tension. The viewer begins within an intimate, almost sheltered woodland environment before being led outward across an immense expanse of atmosphere. Kensett thus constructs the experience of Western vastness incrementally rather than instantaneously, allowing the landscape to unfold slowly before the eye.

The composition of the present work reveals Kensett's consummate manipulation of recession, scale, color, and light. The dark foreground occupies the lower quarter of the canvas, providing a weighted foundation against which the luminous passages above appear almost weightless, while small pools and rivulets of water form a broken diagonal that subtly directs the eye toward the central tree and distant mountains. Successive horizontal bands of wooded foreground, open valley, foothills, the Rocky Mountains, and expansive sky establish a carefully calibrated progression into depth, interrupted by the irregular silhouette of the central tree, whose branches extend laterally into the sky to unite foreground and distance. Kensett further emphasizes recession through a gradual transition from deep olive greens, browns, and near-black tones in the foreground to muted greens, ochres, and autumnal reds in the middle distance, before the Rockies emerge through delicate blue-gray, violet, and rose hues beneath a sky of soft blue-green, peach, salmon, pink, and lavender. Rather than employing a dramatic source of illumination, Kensett diffuses light throughout the atmosphere, allowing it to function as the unifying substance of the landscape. The central tree is particularly important to this effect: rendered with greater specificity at its base, its foliage becomes increasingly indistinct as it rises into the luminous sky, mediating between the tangible foreground and atmospheric distance. Through a carefully controlled interplay of near and far, dark and light, vertical and horizontal, and tangible and ethereal forms, Kensett achieves the tonal harmony and equilibrium characteristic of his finest mature landscapes.

Scene Near Greeley, Colorado ultimately represents a remarkable synthesis of the two geographical poles of Kensett's career: the refined Luminist aesthetic he developed in the East and the monumental natural forms he encountered in the West. Painted shortly before his death in December 1872, the work belongs to a period in which Kensett achieved an extraordinary economy of means and a profound sensitivity to the expressive possibilities of atmosphere. The monumental scale of the present work permitted Kensett to evoke the breadth of the Colorado wilderness while maintaining an intimacy and meditative stillness characteristic of his finest work. Like his celebrated views of the New England coast, Scene Near Greeley, Colorado ultimately concerns not topography alone but perception itself—the experience of looking across space as solid forms gradually dissolve into light. The darkened earth of the foreground, the solitary tree, the distant blue-violet Rockies and the rose-colored sky are brought into a single, harmonious whole. In doing so, Kensett transformed one of the grandest subjects available to a nineteenth-century American landscape painter into something quieter and perhaps more profound. Rather than overwhelm the viewer with an interpretation of the American West as spectacle, Scene Near Greeley, Colorado invites sustained contemplation, demonstrating Kensett's singular ability to locate sublimity in stillness, distance, and atmosphere.

This oil study is a view southwest into richly sunset-stained, dense atmosphere, vignetted by a stony, forested foreground at the left, the distinctive overlapping Shawangunk ridges in the right middle-distance, and an arc of brilliantly colored clouds overhead. Striking and memorable, a tour de force of color, it also perfectly exemplifies Gifford's extraordinary ability to capture in a small format, a vast air-filled space.

This is one of a long series of drawings and paintings by Gifford inspired by the Shawangunk Mountains, just south of the Catskills. The earliest documented is a study of rocks dated August 1850 (MC29; Sale I #1), followed by several works that culminated in a large oval distant view, 41 by 34 inches, exhibited in 1854 at the National Academy as #383, Shawangunk Mountains (and mistakenly listed in the Memorial Catalogue as #55, Sunset in the Catskills). Another group of paintings, based on drawings of 1861 and 1864 (Fogg Art Museum Sketchbooks of 1860–1863, 1863–1865, and 1864) resulted in a lost National Academy exhibition piece of 1865, also titled Shawangunk Mountains (#349; MC375), which was listed by the artist among his "Chief Pictures" [Gifford letter to Frothingham, 1874 and 1880, published in Poetic Landscape (University of Delaware Press, 1987), p. 328)]. Drawings done on a return visit to the Shawangunks in October 1875 (Sketchbook of 1873–1879, Vassar College), in addition to some of the 'Sixties material, preceded a final series of paintings, including the current work.

The known 'Sixties paintings are views due west toward the overlapping Shawangunk ridges that include "The Traps" (rocky cliffs favored by climbers), with the recognizable, graceful contours of their south facing profile now located beyond the foreground in the left third of the format, and layers of air measuring the space. The lost exhibition piece of 1865, 30 by 48 inches, was likely preceded by The Shawangunk Mountains, a Sketch, 9 by 16 inches, in which two figures on a foreground table rock, one seated, one standing, enjoy the view. Here the late afternoon sun in haze, near center, anchors the composition and provides pervasive, unifying color opalescence. Two of the pencil drawings of September 1864 try effects of clouds that emphasize the southwestern light, anticipating the later concept. 

The painting under consideration is one of Gifford's several known Shawangunk interpretations of the 'Seventies, all exploring the rich coloring of autumn foliage at dusk. Its foreground contains rocks, pines, deciduous trees and dead trunks, dark browns with limited golden highlights and small dabs of green, nearly silhouetted against the luminous distance. These colors are slightly lightened in the middle-distance and receive a wash of cool grays that set the escarpment behind a veil of air. Similar cool grays convey dusk in the distance and in the overcast sky. In the foreground two small white marks, a dot over a curved line, conjure a figure emerging from behind a rock en route to the vantage point. A smaller, looser oil sketch in the Smithsonian Museum of American Art, 3 1/8 by 5 3/8 inches (MC 374; Loan Collection #90), likely the earliest version of this group, contains a possible indication of that figure (particularly his hat); a larger version, 8 1/2 by 14 3/4 inches (Estate Sale II, either #69 or #82), clarifies it. In all the 'Seventies paintings the setting sun is located toward the right edge, stressed in this version with impasto yellow. In a shadowed indentation among the mountain ridges, tiny golden dabs represent water reflecting the sunlight. These are echoed in the hazy distance, where they entice the eye into depth and upward across the clouds. Here red orange impasto highlights vigorously concentrate the softer orange tones dispersed throughout, exemplifying Gifford's mastery of color.

In one Shawangunk drawing of 1875, broken, repeated horizontal lines evoke the indefinite aerial transition from land to sky featured in the later paintings. The three smallest of the 'Seventies interpretations retain the dark clouds and shifted distant focus of the two 'Sixties drawings, now overlapped for emphasis by vertically elongated pines at the left and bracketed at the right by the escarpment profile. The largest known and probably final version, 14 by 24 inches, Twilight in the Shawangunk Mountains, (MC 657, sold in 1877), demonstrates formal resolution throughout, in keeping with Gifford's stepwise process of developing imagery. Its clouds are distilled to five orange puffs directing the eye to the first sliver of a new moon barely visible in the now pellucid sky. Reflecting Gifford's philosophy, the single climbing figure is now standing on the table rock that had been inhabited by two figures in 1864, sharing the viewer's—and the artist's—experience: an ecstatic moment of aesthetic perfection, with spiritual implications.

Thomas Moran was a defining figure in American landscape painting, celebrated above all for his monumental interpretations of the American West but equally indebted throughout his career to the landscapes and artistic traditions of his native England. Born in Bolton in 1837 to Mary (née Higson) and Thomas Moran Sr., Moran's origins in England were short lived. Forced out of the country due to widespread poverty and near famine, Thomas Moran Sr. arrived in America in 1842, followed by his wife and seven children in 1844. The family eventually settled in Philadelphia and in the years that followed, the Moran children prospered. Moran's older brother Edward Moran (1829-1901) became a successful artist in his own right, paving the way for Moran to begin his own artistic studies. Beginning in 1853, Moran worked as an engraver for Scattergood and Telfer in Philadelphia and started his studies under Paul Gottlieb Weber (1823-1916) and James Hamilton (1819-1878), two men who would later be regarded by Moran as fundamental mentors to his development as an artist. (N.K. Anderson, Thomas Moran, exhibition catalogue, Washington, D.C., 1997, p. 25) 

Moran's artistic outlook was profoundly shaped by his study of English and European landscape painting traditions, particularly the work of J.M.W. Turner (1775-1851), whose atmospheric effects, luminous color, and expressive treatment of nature left a lasting impression on him. In 1862, Moran traveled to England with his brother Edward to study Turner's work firsthand. He copied Turner's paintings and watercolors at the National Gallery in London and traveled through the English countryside, often seeking out places that Turner himself had depicted. This period of study would remain fundamental to the development of Moran's artistic techniques and approach to landscape painting for the remainder of his career.

Moran's defining success is often associated with the American West, particularly following his participation in the 1871 Hayden Geological Survey of the Yellowstone region, yet his engagement with the English landscape remained a constant throughout his career. His lifelong admiration for Turner provided him with a conceptual framework through which he approached both European and American environs, drawing him to landscapes where water, mountains, weather, and shifting light could be combined into dramatic, atmospheric compositions. He painted subjects throughout England and Scotland, with a particular interest in the rugged coast of Cornwall, which he visited in 1906, following in Turner's footsteps at Tintagel and Land's End. (T. Wilkins, Thomas Moran: Artist of the Mountains, Norman, Oklahoma, 1966, p. 227) Rather than simply documenting these sites, Moran adapted and combined observed elements, transforming castles, coastal villages, mountains, lakes, and turbulent skies into evocative fixtures in a romantic world to convey the emotional character of the landscape. This approach remained central to his later work, as he continued to explore dramatic skies, luminous effects, deep space, and rapidly changing weather even as American subjects dominated his oeuvre.

In contrast to Moran's depictions of the monumental wilderness of Yellowstone or the American Southwest, The Stronghold, painted in 1920, evokes the romantic character of an English landscape. A tranquil body of water recedes toward a distant shore, where a small, fortified structure stands beneath an imposing range of mountains. Above the scene, heavy clouds gather and break, allowing warm light to illuminate portions of the mountains and architecture. The effect is distinctly atmospheric, with the landscape appearing to exist in a moment of transition between storm and sunlight. Moran's handling of the scene is particularly indebted to the visual language he absorbed from Turner more than half a century earlier. The dramatic sky, brilliant passages of reflected light, warm ocher and rose tones set against deep blue-gray clouds, and the deliberately heightened relationship between atmosphere and topography all demonstrate Moran's enduring interest in the expressive possibilities of landscape. The architectural "stronghold" depicted is small in relation to its surroundings, functioning less as a precise architectural study than as a poetic focal point within an expansive natural world.

Painted in the final years of his life, The Stronghold represents the culmination of a dialogue with the English landscape that Moran began during his formative years in England. The present work demonstrates that Moran's artistic identity is not confined to his celebrated images of the American West. The same imagination that Moran employed to transform Yellowstone into a vision of the sublime is applied to the mountains, waters, architecture, and storm-filled skies of England. In The Stronghold, Moran returns to the Romantic vocabulary that first captivated him in Turner's paintings while bringing to it the experience of a lifetime spent painting some of the world's most dramatic scenery. The result is a work in which English subject matter, Turneresque atmosphere, and Moran's uniquely American conception of the sublime converge, revealing the remarkable continuity of an artistic vision that endured throughout his career.

In 1849, Worthington Whittredge embarked on the European travels that would profoundly shape his development as a landscape painter. After studying and working in Germany, where he became closely associated with the Düsseldorf School, Whittredge traveled to Italy in 1856, joining a circle of American expatriate artists studying and working in Rome, including Albert Bierstadt (1830-1902), Sanford Robinson Gifford (1823-1880), and William Stanley Haseltine (1835-1900). (A.F. Janson, Worthington Whittredge, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1989, pp. 54-58) Whittredge remained in Italy until 1859, devoting much of his time to sketching the surrounding countryside, particularly the expansive Roman Campagna. The present work, painted in 1857, consummately reflects Whittredge's union of the academic principles he absorbed in Düsseldorf with his direct observation of the Italian landscape. The broad horizons, distant hills, and atmospheric light of the Italian countryside provided Whittredge with an ideal setting in which to explore tonal harmony, spatial recession, and the spiritual transcendence of nature. Ultimately, Whittredge's years spent in Italy were instrumental in establishing the distinct vocabulary and mature technical approach that he would carry with him back to America in 1859, where he would go on to become an important figure within the Hudson River School.

PROPERTY FROM A PRIVATE COLLECTION, ATLANTA, GEORGIAALBERT BIERSTADT (1830-1902)
Mountain with Clouds 
signed 'ABierstadt.' (lower left)
oil on paper laid down on canvas
15 x 11 5/8 in. (38.1 x 29.5 cm.)

Provenance
Frances Aronson Fine Art, Atlanta, Georgia, by 1992. 
Acquired by the present owner from the above, March 1992.

We would like to thank Melissa Webster Speidel, President of the Bierstadt Foundation and Director of the Albert Bierstadt catalogue raisonné project, for her kind assistance cataloguing this lot and for preparing the following commentary. This work is included in the database being compiled for her forthcoming catalogue raisonné of the artist's work.

The painting depicts a rugged mountain enshrouded in clouds, with snow nestled between its rocky pinnacles and loosely brushed passages of green and brown suggesting vegetation along the slopes. As part of his artistic process, Bierstadt painted plein air oil sketches and studies of nature that he later referred to in his studio when creating finished paintings. Typically, he focused on a particular element of the landscape, rendering it more specifically while treating surrounding passages more broadly. In this sketch, Bierstadt concentrated on the rock formations, clouds and light, recording how the peaks emerge and disappear into the surrounding atmosphere. He defined the craggy pinnacles with short, directional strokes of warm color and used touches of lighter paint to indicate snow between the rock formations and areas illuminated by sunlight, while the clouds are more broadly and softly handled. 

The subject work fits within a recognizable body of Bierstadt's practice. A comparable sketch is Cloud Study with Mountain Peaks (Private collection). As in the subject work, the degree of finish was determined by what the artist was studying. In Cloud Study with Mountain Peaks, Bierstadt focused on the upper region of the composition, more carefully describing the clouds and mountain peaks while rendering the lower areas with looser, less defined brushwork. This selective degree of finish reflects his interest in recording particular effects or features of the landscape rather than developing every part of the composition equally. In other sketches, [such as Gathering Storm (Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Washington, D.C., accession no. 66.503)] Bierstadt rendered the entire composition in broad brushstrokes as he worked quickly to capture specific atmospheric conditions in the landscape. (M.W. Speidel, President of the Bierstadt Foundation and Director of the Albert Bierstadt catalogue raisonné project, unpublished letter, September 7, 2026)

ALBERT BIERSTADT (1830-1902)
Lake Tahoe, California 
signed with conjoined initials 'AB.' (lower right)
oil on paper laid down on board
7 1/4 x 9 1/2 in. (18.4 x 24.1 cm.)
Painted circa 1871.

Provenance
(possibly) George McMurry, Glendale, California. 
Frances Aronson Fine Art, Atlanta, Georgia, by 1992. 
Acquired by the present owner from the above, March 1992.

We would like to thank Melissa Webster Speidel, President of the Bierstadt Foundation and Director of the Albert Bierstadt catalogue raisonné project, for her kind assistance cataloguing this lot and for preparing the following commentary. This work is included in the database being compiled for her forthcoming catalogue raisonné of the artist's work.

The painting depicts a figure in a canoe on a body of water, a rocky shore behind him, mountains in the distance and a blue sky with clouds above. Bierstadt visited Lake Tahoe at least three times during his career. The first time was in 1863 while traveling with writer Fitz Hugh Ludlow who described their arrival to the lake after traveling through the deserts of Utah and Nevada as being "translated . . . out of the infernal world into heaven." (F.H. Ludlow, "Among the Mormons," The Atlantic Monthly, April 1864, vol. XIII, no. LXXVIII, p. 495) The subsequent trips were in 1871 and 1872 when the artist was residing in California and exploring and sketching the Sierra Nevada and California's coast.

Approximately thirty Lake Tahoe paintings by Bierstadt have been identified, some studies, some finished oils, and a dozen more are thought to be of Lake Tahoe. The artist painted the studies and sketches, like the subject work, en plein air and later referred to them in his studio when creating finished oils. In these sketches, Bierstadt often concentrated on a particular aspect of the landscape, such as the lighting, a rock or cloud formation or the composition itself. In the subject work, he recorded the overlapping landforms and employed atmospheric perspective to create a sense of depth. He frequently used these devices to establish spatial recession in his landscapes, as seen, for example in Lake Tahoe, California (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, accession no. 47.1243).

The subject work also displays Bierstadt's characteristic handling of paint, with horizontal painterly brushwork describing the foreground water and background sky, shorter vertical strokes describing the landforms, and dry stippling suggesting the greenery at left. The combination of these techniques with the painting's subject, palette and spatial construction is consistent with Bierstadt's plein-air oil sketches of the landscape.

Everett Shinn's fascination with the theater is a hallmark of his oeuvre that he revisited innumerable times and across a variety of mediums. With the theater as his muse, he explored the manipulation of movement, performance, and the dramatic effects of artificial light in a given composition. Shinn frequently depicted performers onstage, drawing upon his intimate familiarity with the theatrical world as both an artist and an active participant in New York's cultural life. This mastery of setting and draftsmanship is evident in Gallatin's observation: "Very real they are: we might almost imagine ourselves looking in upon the actual scene." (A. E. Gallatin, "Studio-Talk," The International Studio, New York, November 1906, vol. 30, no. 117, p. 86.) His theatrical subjects were particularly well suited to pastel, a medium that allowed him to work rapidly and capture the immediacy and transitory character of a performance, enabling the viewer to become a spectator at the show. 

The present work captures two contrasting views in the theater: performers spiritedly dancing onstage and musicians below, energetically playing a tune. Bathed in rich, yellow light, the performers seemingly glow and float above the stage. An almost straight horizontal line divides the composition, revealing the source of the music to which the figures above dance. Rendered with rapid, vigorous strokes, the musicians appear in a deliberately animated state, their gestural energy conveying the movement and immediacy of the performance. The work belongs to a later period of Shinn's sustained engagement with theatrical subjects, when performers, stages, and music halls remained central to his imagery. The work exemplifies Shinn's enduring fascination with the theater, translating the fleeting interplay of light, movement, and music into a vibrant composition.

Landscape Sketch and Brunette Nude, Striped Blanket: A Double-Sided Work offers an opportunity to consider the artistic practice of one of the most important artists of the twentieth century. Painted on opposite sides of the same canvas are a Gloucester landscape dating from 1917 and a nude dating from 1928–30. Separated by more than a decade, the two compositions reflect distinct chapters in Sloan's oeuvre and reveal the artist's return to an earlier support long after its original use. The double-sided nature of the work provides a tangible link between Sloan's Gloucester landscapes of the 1910s and his later explorations of the nude in the 1920s, uniting two otherwise disparate moments in his career on a single support.

From 1914 to 1918, John Sloan found in Gloucester's windswept coast a rare and sustaining source of inspiration. Sloan spent five consecutive summers renting Red Cottage near Rocky Neck in East Gloucester. He devoted himself to exploring the city's rocky shores, sketching its working waterfront, and absorbing the mutable light that danced across the water of the harbor. The landscape's natural beauty became a living canvas, offering Sloan an arena in which to probe the interplay of color and texture and to explore form with a freedom that invigorated his brush. In Gloucester, the seascape, main streets, and scenes of everyday life were not merely recorded but continually reimagined and transformed through his evolving artistic vision. Sloan was not alone in his admiration for Gloucester's coastal landscape. American artists such as Fitz Hugh Lane (1804–1865), Winslow Homer (1836–1910), Childe Hassam (1859–1935), Maurice Prendergast (1858–1924), Stuart Davis (1892–1964) and Edward Hopper (1882–1967) likewise turned to the North Shore, each capturing its distinctive atmosphere and quiet rhythms in their own unique way. Together, these artists helped establish Gloucester as one of the most enduring artistic centers in American art.

Following the heralded Armory Show in 1913, Sloan's artistic approach underwent a decisive shift after encountering works by Paul Cézanne (1839–1906), Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890), and Pablo Picasso (1881–1973). Reflecting on this experience, he later remarked, "I realized that they had a 'habit of working.' My way had been, since I had so little time to work for myself, to wait until I had an idea for a picture. Of course, I painted some portraits of friends and did some small landscapes when I had a week or two off in the summer, but at the age of forty I realized that I needed some new ways to keep at work. I saw that the European artists kept themselves going, with any kind of subject, landscape, or portrait, or still life (in any style). This method produces more work, more 'studies'; but it also leads to the discovery of new motivations. I made up my mind to save enough money to take a few months off to paint landscape in Gloucester." (The John Sloan Exhibit, exhibition catalogue, Lock Haven, Pennsylvania, 1970, p. 5) This resolve marked a turning point, enabling Sloan to devote sustained attention to landscape painting and ultimately to broaden his painterly practice.

During his Massachusetts summers, Sloan prioritized painting en plein air, using the immediacy of direct observation outdoors to further refine his approach. At this time, he engaged deeply with Hardesty Maratta's color system through published writings, as well as through extensive discussions with Robert Henri (1865–1929), while drawing upon the rich variety of subjects available to him. These summers in Gloucester marked an extraordinary enhancement of Sloan's creative output. 292 paintings emerged from this period, including the present work. (John Sloan: Gloucester Days, exhibition catalogue, Gloucester, Massachusetts, 2015, p. 12) Each captures the vitality, subtle rhythms, and luminous moods of a landscape he had come to know intimately. It was a moment when experimentation and observation coalesced, producing a body of work that not only affirms Sloan's command of realism but also conveys a heightened sense of immediacy and presence. Landscape Sketch exhibits his prowess by allowing topographical fixtures in the landscape to dictate subtle movements on the canvas. Perched atop a high cliff, Sloan chose to depict three figures and a dog trotting along a dirt path. In the far distance, houses are stacked alongside one another in a similar manner to some of the rock formations in the immediate foreground. These interplays of shape and color speak to key compositional hallmarks of Sloan's Gloucester period.

Landscape Sketch offers a lens into the evolution of Sloan's en plein air painting, while Brunette Nude, Striped Blanket provides a glimpse into the stylistic evolution of a subject he had first explored seriously in the 1910s. In Gist of Art, Sloan writes, "I don't like a nude that looks too much like human flesh. I think it might better have a dry, hard look, be sculpture with color-textures like a piece of bronze." (J. Sloan, John Sloan on Drawing and Painting (Gist of Art), Mineola, New York, 1944, p. 87) 

In his first serious exploration of the nude on canvas dating from the 1910s, Sloan's painterly handling of the subject, coupled with a soft palette, produced a softly modeled, comparatively restrained figure. Brunette Nude, Striped Blanket illustrates the evolution in the artist's style as it is a "linear, tightly controlled painting...Sloan twisted and turned the figure in order to obtain a more dynamic organization of space." (G. Holcomb III, A Catalogue Raisonné of the Paintings of John Sloan, 1900-1913, Ph.D. dissertation, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, 1972, p. 56) The model's dynamic pose is further contrasted through the horizontal striped blanket she sits atop. During the late 1920s, Sloan also incorporated lines and cross-hatching into his figuration, which is also evident in the present work.

Landscape Sketch and Brunette Nude, Striped Blanket: A Double-Sided Work speaks to the evolution of John Sloan's artistic exploration. The former documents his search for new ways of sustaining his artistic practice, while the latter shows a deviation from the artist's earlier conceptualization of the nude. It is fitting then that this work was once in the collection of Ruth Martin, a friend and former sitter of John Sloan who at one point amassed the largest collection of the artist's works in private hands. Even though the two sides are separated by more than a decade, the work informs our understanding of Sloan, revealing how his style evolved and matured across distinct periods of his career.
