Constructed between 1931 and 1936, Hoover Dam stands as one of the monumental feats of engineering of the twentieth century and a defining symbol of American industrial progress during the Great Depression. Built across the Colorado River in the Black Canyon, the grandiose concrete dam was conceived to control flooding, provide irrigation and municipal water, and generate hydroelectric power for the surrounding areas. The project was authorized under President Herbert Hoover and officially began in 1931, employing thousands of laborers who worked under arduous and often dangerous conditions to divert the river, excavate the canyon walls, and pour millions of tons of concrete. Completed two years ahead of schedule, the dam illustrated the transformative potential of federally funded public works. Its construction also reflected the economic and social circumstances of the Depression, when major infrastructure projects offered employment and a sense of collective purpose amid widespread hardship.

John R. Grabach's 1937 Hoover Dam triptych documenting its construction reflects the artist's commitment to urban realism and his sustained interest in the dignity and physical demands of working-class life. In the late 1930s, Grabach conceived the composition as a mural, allegedly in the hope of securing a commission for a post office or through the Works Progress Administration (WPA), whose Federal Art Project supported artists and brought art into public spaces during the Depression. Although the mural was never executed, Grabach realized the concept in a triptych painting and a related lithograph known as Construction. The composition transforms physical exertion into a monumental celebration of human labor. The model for one of the figures was reportedly a freight jumper who periodically passed through town and occasionally posed for the artist, underscoring Grabach's practice of drawing inspiration from everyday working people. (John R. Grabach, 1880-1981: Urban America Between the Wars, exhibition catalogue, 1981, p. 17) The painting elevates the laborers from anonymous participants in a vast engineering project to the central protagonists of American industrial achievement, thus highlighting Grabach's interest in capturing images of the working class. Its original conception as a potential public mural also places the work within the broader cultural ambitions of the 1930s, when artists increasingly sought to transform scenes of the American experience into monumental art.

John R. Grabach's oeuvre informs our understanding of American art throughout the twentieth century. Born in 1886, he expressed an interest in drawing from a young age while growing up in Newark, New Jersey. At the age of 18, he decided to enroll in The Art Students League, where his instructors included Kenyon Cox (1856-1919), George Bridgman (1864-1943) and Frank Dumond (1865-1941).

Grabach relocated to New England in 1912, where he found inspiration in the landscape. He captured winter plein air scenes, despite the elements, throughout Massachusetts and Connecticut. During this period, Grabach embraced tonalism and these works enabled him to gain acceptance into premier exhibitions at the Art Institute of Chicago, the Corcoran Gallery of Art and the Carnegie Institute.

In the early 1920s, Grabach took a studio in New York near the Brooklyn Bridge. It was here that he forged his distinctive urban realist style which many art historians have compared to the work of his Ashcan peers. However, "Grabach did not view America through rose colored glasses. Grabach's paintings never portrayed the American dream. He preferred to focus on the American way of life revealing the outgrowth of social conformity." (John R. Grabach: Century Man, exhibition catalogue, New Castle, Pennsylvania, 2006, p. 8) The artist chose to infuse his politics into a great deal of his work from this period, which is evident in The Horizon (Arising).

The Horizon (Arising) was painted as a companion piece in response to the reception of an earlier work, The Fifth Year (1934, Smithsonian American Art Museum, object no. 1979.119.1). The Fifth Year captures Grabach's interpretation of the working class's lifestyle during the Great Depression, five years after the stock market crash of 1929. The desolate conditions evident in this painting contributed to the rise of the Socialist and Communist movements, themes that are evident in The Horizon (Arising). In the present work, Grabach, "depicts an angry group of people bearing various weapons and objects with political connotation forging forward above the cityscape below and beyond the boundaries of America." (John R. Grabach: Century Man, exhibition catalogue, New Castle, Pennsylvania, 2006, p. 9) The group of workers in The Horizon (Arising) carry knives, sickles, and poles fixed with bayonets as they march over New York City, and possibly around the world as critics claim the Eiffel Tower can be seen in the upper right. Both works provide a glimpse into the social history of the 1930s, when American politics highlighted the discontent among the working class and the call for unionization.

N.C. Wyeth maintained a long and productive relationship with the publishing house of Charles Scribner's Sons. Beginning with Wyeth's masterful illustrations for Robert Louis Stevenson's (1850-1894) Treasure Island (1911), Wyeth established a body of work for the publisher that would span several decades. Among the best known are Kidnapped (1913), The Black Arrow (1916), The Boy's King Arthur (1917), The Mysterious Island (1918), The Last of the Mohicans (1919), The Deerslayer (1925), and The Yearling (1939). 

Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings' (1896-1953) third novel, The Yearling, was published in March of 1938. The novel follows Jody Baxter, a young boy, and his family in the backwoods of Florida in the 1870s. The novel was a success, becoming the number one best seller in America for twenty-three consecutive weeks with over 250,000 copies sold in 1938 alone. The Yearling went on to win the Pulitzer Prize in 1939, and the Scribner's edition, for which Wyeth produced thirteen panels, among them the present work, was published that same year.

Near the end of Chapter XIV, Jody's father, Penny, is bitten by a rattlesnake. Wyeth chooses to depict not the dramatic moment of the bite but rather the solemn aftermath in The Vigil. "It seemed to Jody that he was alone with his father. The vigil was in his hands. If he kept awake, and labored for breath with the tortured sleeper, breathing with him and for him, he could keep him alive. He drew a breath as deep as the ones his father was drawing. It made him dizzy. He was light-headed and his stomach was empty. He knew he would feel better if he should eat, but he could not swallow. He sat down on the floor and leaned his head against the side of the bed. He began to think back over the day, as though he walked a road backward. He could not help but feel a greater security here beside his father, than in the stormy night. Many things, he realized, would be terrible alone that were not terrible when he was with Penny." (M.K. Rawlings, The Yearling, New York, 1938, p. 158)

As is the case with N.C. Wyeth's most successful works, the painting exists in the interstices of the text. The figures are placed by the author, and Wyeth enhances the narrative by depicting the moment just after everyone seemingly has slipped into sleep. Wyeth's use of chiaroscuro lighting along a strong diagonal plane defines the picture. Interestingly, Wyeth echoes this structure in color using the cool blue and green tones in the basin, Jody's pants, the coverlet, and the coverlet's reflection in the window in a parallel diagonal. The three figures are a study of the ages of man; the young boy is at the bedside, the father lies gravely ill and the elderly man has nodded off in an exhausted slumber following the intense time at death's door. The shadow of the rarely sober old doctor is like a fourth figure in the composition continuing the strong diagonal and perhaps providing a visual reference to death looking in but not staying. As Penny says to Jody the next morning, "Ol' Death gone thievin' elsewhere. But wa'n't it a close squeak!" (M.K. Rawlings, The Yearling, p. 164) Despite the sleeping figures, Wyeth conveys both tension and calm simultaneously, a testament to his mature command of mood and narrative expression. The Vigil does not simply illustrate Rawlings' story; it enriches the psychological and emotional experience of the reader.
